The '''1891 Canadian federal election''' was held on March 5, 1891, to elect members of the [[House of Commons of Canada]] of the [[7th Canadian Parliament|7th Parliament]] of [[Canada]]. It was won by the [[Conservative Party of Canada (historical)|Conservative Party]] of [[Prime Minister of Canada|Prime Minister]] Sir [[John A. Macdonald]]. 
[[File:John A Macdonald election poster 1891.jpg|upright|thumb|An election poster in support of the [[Conservative Party of Canada (historical)|Conservative]] party from 1891.]]
The main issue of the 1891 campaign was Macdonald's [[National Policy]], a policy of protective tariffs. The Liberals supported [[reciprocity (Canadian politics)|reciprocity]] (free trade) with the [[United States]]. Canadian voters would return to the issue of free trade 20 years later in the [[1911 Canadian federal election|1911 federal election]].

Macdonald led a Conservative campaign emphasizing stability, and retained the Conservatives' majority in the [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]]. It was a close election and he campaigned hard. Macdonald died a few months after the election, which led to his succession by four different Conservative Prime Ministers until the [[1896 Canadian federal election|1896 election]].

It was [[Wilfrid Laurier]]'s first election as leader of the [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberals]]. Although he lost the election, he increased the Liberals' support. He returned in 1896 to win a solid majority, despite losing the popular vote.

The [[Quebec nationalism|Nationalist Party]] won a seat in Quebec. Dorchester riding elected [[Cyrille-Émile Vaillancourt]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://lop.parl.ca/sites/ParlInfo/default/en_CA/People/Profile?personId=6267 | title=Profile }}</ref>

'''Acclamations:'''

The following Members of Parliament were elected by acclamation;
* British Columbia: 1 Conservative, 1 Liberal-Conservative
* Manitoba: 1 Conservative
* Ontario: 1 Conservative
* Quebec: 1 Conservative, 2 Liberal, 1 Nationalist
